findings.title: Leitner System: Algorithm Design and Performance
findings.key_finding: The Leitner system's O(n) sorting is simple but lacks adaptive scheduling. Cards are grouped by box, not by individual difficulty curves. Works well for vocabulary but struggles with conceptual programming topics where partial knowledge is common.
findings.confidence_note: Well-established algorithm with 50+ years of research backing.

findings.title: SM-2 and SuperMemo: Interval Scheduling Mathematics
findings.key_finding: SM-2 is the foundation of most modern spaced-repetition software (Anki uses a modified SM-2). The algorithm is deterministic — same inputs always produce the same schedule. Weakness: the easiness factor can collapse to minimum for difficult cards, creating review pile-ups. SM-17/18 address this with statistical models but are proprietary.
findings.confidence_note: SM-2 is open and well-understood. SM-17+ are closed-source; findings based on published papers only.

findings.title: Learning Outcomes: SRS vs Traditional Study for Programming
findings.key_finding: SRS excels at declarative knowledge (API names, syntax patterns, error codes) but underperforms for procedural knowledge (algorithm design, debugging strategies). Students who combined SRS with project-based practice outperformed both pure-SRS and pure-project groups by 28%. The optimal ratio appears to be ~30% SRS / 70% active coding.
findings.confidence_note: Meta-analysis quality varies; individual study sizes were 20-80 participants.

findings.title: User Experience Research: Why Learners Abandon SRS
findings.key_finding: The 'review debt' problem is the #1 UX failure of current SRS tools for programming. When a learner misses 3 days, returning to 200+ pending reviews feels overwhelming. Successful long-term users (>1yr) all reported the same coping strategy: ruthless deck pruning and a 'max 20 min/day' hard cap.
findings.confidence_note: Self-reported survey data; potential survivorship bias in the 'successful users' subgroup.

findings.title: Against Spaced Repetition for Programming: A Critical Review
findings.key_finding: The core argument: you don't get better at programming by remembering more facts — you get better by solving more problems. SRS optimizes for recall, but programming fluency requires transfer (applying knowledge in novel contexts). No SRS system effectively tests transfer. The author proposes 'spaced practice' (revisiting problem types at intervals) as superior to 'spaced repetition' (reviewing cards at intervals). Key distinction: practice generates knowledge; repetition preserves it.
findings.confidence_note: Position paper, not empirical study. Arguments are well-constructed but unverified experimentally.
